name: Extending Context Window of Large Language Models via Positional Interpolation
problem: Extending a transformer's context window by letting it see position indices beyond those it was trained on (extrapolation) produces catastrophically high attention scores that can destroy self-attention entirely.
mechanism: Instead of extrapolating, INTERPOLATE: linearly down-scale the input position indices so the extended window maps onto the original trained range (positions p -> p / s for scale factor s). The paper's theoretical contribution is a bound showing the upper bound on the interpolated attention is at least ~600x smaller than that of extrapolation, which is why interpolation is stable and extrapolation is not. No architecture change - the same weights and the same kernels work, which is the point.
speedup_reported: NOT A PERFORMANCE CLAIM. The one quantitative claim in the abstract is theoretical, not a speedup: the upper bound of interpolation is at least ~600x smaller than that of extrapolation. Quality result: models extended via Position Interpolation retain the original architecture and can reuse most pre-existing optimization and infrastructure.
notes:
arXiv ID 2306.15595 verified via abs-page citation_title/citation_date on 2026-10-03; title matches. venue=arxiv-preprint: no venue claim in the arXiv comment (only 'Fix template issues'); OpenReview search for this exact title returns only a LATER paper by an overlapping team ('Exploring Context Window of LLMs via Decomposable Law', NeurIPS 2024) - a different paper, do not conflate. adoption=in-upstream-engine: position interpolation is the 'linear' rope_type, present in transformers ROPE_INIT_FUNCTIONS as 'linear' -> _compute_linear_scaling_rope_parameters, and in vLLM as LinearScalingRotaryEmbedding. Because the method is a pure position-index remap, ANY engine that accepts a scaling factor supports it without a new kernel - the strongest form of adoption and the reason this record is worth keeping. Note this is the paper that motivated YaRN and LongRoPE, both recorded separately here.
